title: Generics + Collections
story: You've mastered generics and you've mastered collections — but the real magic happens when you COMBINE them. Write a function once that works with Vec, Map, ANY collection of ANY type. This is the synthesis that makes your code feel like a superpower.
why: Generic functions over collections let you write operations like count, contains, and find once and apply them to any type — the ultimate expression of DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself) at the type level.
analogy: Generic functions over collections are like vending machines that accept any coin — pennies, nickels, dimes, quarters. The machine mechanism (Vec operations) works the same regardless of the coin type (T). Insert coin, push button, get snack — the coin type doesn't change the machine's behavior.
try_it: Write a `merge[T]` function that takes two Vec[T] and returns a new Vec[T] with all items from both. Test with Int, Str, and Bool. Then write `take[T](items: &Vec[T], n: Int) -> Vec[T]` that returns the first n items. What operations can you do generically vs what requires knowing about T? Make a list — it'll prepare you for L6 interfaces!
tips: Operations on Vec (push, get, len) work for any T — use these freely in generic functions
Operations on T (compare, add, display) need interface constraints — L6 will unlock this
Multiple type parameters: `fn zip[K, V](...) -> Map[K, V]` works when you need two generic types
common_mistakes: Trying to compare generic values with `==` — not all types support equality; this requires interface bounds (L6)
Forgetting `[T]` on functions that take Vec[T] — the compiler needs to know T is a type parameter
Mixing generic types — `fn foo[T](a: Vec[T], b: Vec[T])` requires both Vecs to have the same T
